Gracias Por Invitar · Living Project Portal 
 G.P.I

 Team 9 Project Portal

 Gracias Por Invitar , Living Project Portal, Sprint 1
 Market Research
 Five candidate problems, 51 customer interviews in two phases, and how the team narrowed to one.
 Version 1.3 , Final , revised Sep 21, 2026 Owner Jazmin Huerta Team Samuel Alderete, Jazmin Huerta, Christian Lopez-Matulessy, Emmanuel Saenz, Oscar Vargas Course CS 4390/5388 Software Project Management , The University of Texas at El Paso , Fall 2026 Web https://gpi-portal.onrender.com/sprint-1/market-research/ Summary

 The team started Sprint 1 with five candidate problems and talked to 51 people about them across two phases. During Phase 1, 26 interviews were held across all five project candidates, but they were narrowed to two. In Phase 2, the team performed 25 interviews on the two selected candidate projects. The results showed that the nutrition candidate (that had looked strongest in Phase 1) did not hold up after applying it to a bigger sample of people, while the events candidate did. The team is moving forward with Candidate 3: an event tracker that will inform people of what is happening in El Paso and Juárez before it happens. 

 1. Aggregating the Findings

 Method note: interviews followed Mom Test rules.

 1.1 Manual logging dies within weeks

 This was the one finding that repeated across all the app candidates. In the finance conversations, people would stop logging their expenses after a month. In nutrition, all five Phase 1 participants had quit a tracking app within one to four weeks. In addition, 13 of the interviewed people in Phase 2 (for this same app candidate), four described quitting for similar reasons: forgotten snacks, or homemade food they couldn't estimate. The conclusion reached was that a product that needs the user to enter/track things every day eventually stops being utilized.

 1.2 The information exists; it does not reach people

 For events specifically, nobody said El Paso lacks things to do, but that they do not hear about them. Announcements are usually found on the Instagram pages of the venue, the organizer, or event/news accounts such as FitFam, and only reach people already following the right ones: "Unless you follow the exact business or page hosting it, you might never see it." People without social media, or who use it lightly, are cut off almost entirely.

 1.3 Free resources exist already

 For some of the app candidates, enough free alternatives exist, so we couldn't identify any market gaps that would make it worth it to introduce a new service doing the same thing; these needs were already being satisfied. For example, an interviewee mentioned that their credit card already categorizes purchases. Several Phase 2 nutrition participants find MyFitnessPal encouraging and sufficient. Similarly, the streaming problem is already served by JustWatch and Reelgood at no cost. Lastly, for the event tracker, regular Instagram users found no need for another event platform; however, we identified a gap for people who don't own any social media profiles.

 2. Top Pick: An Events Hub for El Paso/Juárez

 Our assumption

 People find it hard to find events and places to go to in El Paso/Juárez, often finding out after the events have already happened.

 Phase 1 results

 All six interview participants could name an event they had missed, which put the problem on the board. But only two of six said it happens often, and three said they do not look for events at all since they get the information through a social media feed or by word of mouth. When compared to Candidate 2's five-for-five Phase 1 result, this looked like the weaker survivor, and the team carried it into Phase 2 mainly because the missed-event stories were so specific.

 Phase 2 results

 The question set was focused on past experiences: the last public event attended and how they heard about it, where they look for details, the last time they found out too late and how often that happens, and one open question about what they would change. Twelve conversations, six with working professionals rather than students.

 # Participant How often they find out too late What they would change 
 1 UTEP student, regular at markets/concerts Once or twice a month One place to see everything happening that weekend 
 2 College student who plans weekends with friends "Pretty often" Hearing about things at least a week ahead 
 3 UTEP student who goes out often "Enough that I've noticed" El Paso and Juárez together; discovery beyond the feed 
 4 Student with limited social media use Every couple of months Events by date, without needing Instagram 
 5 Student with a heavily curated Instagram feed Rarely (weak signal) Filtering by type of event 
 6 Software specialist Could not say, "I'm not aware of them" Tell it your interests, have it tell you what's on 
 7 Social worker A few times a year A standardized source 
 8 Attorney A couple of times Advertising beyond social media 
 9 County worker Never because spouse finds events for them No suggestion 
 10 Victim advocate About once a year A weekly round-up/calendar from official accounts 
 11 Paralegal Rarely; follows enough accounts One source; interest-based email digest 
 12 Aerospace engineer, regular event-goer At least once a month A central listing, like the weekly page that stopped 

 Six of twelve miss events they would have attended on a recurring basis (monthly, to a few times a year), four say rarely, and two gave no usable frequency.

 Seven of twelve, in their own words and without being offered the idea, asked for a single place to see what is coming: "there isn't one place where I can just see everything happening that weekend"; "El Paso lacks a one-source location"; "there used to be a page that would put all of the events that were going on every week, but they stopped doing that." Three asked for interest-based filtering, two asked for about a week of lead time, and two asked for reach beyond social media.

 Who is underserved?

 Word-of-mouth dependents: Of the twelve Phase 2 conversations, five describe someone else as their primary way of hearing about events, making this the largest of the three groups, though not a majority.

 People with little or no social media: Two Phase 2 participants and one Phase 1 participant had this issue. Google gives them "tourist attractions or places that are always open instead of actual events happening that weekend." They are the clearest gap but also outliers in some way.

 People with a curated feed: Even though they were able to find events easily, they still mentioned wanting to filter by interest.

 Where people look today, and where this fails

 Channel What it does well Where it fails, in participants' words 
 Instagram / TikTok Everything eventually gets posted Only shows what you already follow; "keeps showing me the same type of stuff" 
 FitFam and similar accounts One place many locals check Still one account's curation; non-followers never see it 
 Facebook events Notifies when friends are going Limited to whoever posts there 
 Google Finds details once you know the name Returns places, not events: "doesn't show me what's actually happening" 
 Ticketmaster / artist accounts Big shows Only big shows, only if you follow the artist; tickets gone before you hear 
 Flyers, QR codes, road signs Reach people offline Localized to one coffee shop's wall or one road 
 A weekly listing page Exactly what people asked for It stopped or people aren't aware of the resource 

 What the evidence does not support

 That everyone has this problem: four of twelve Phase 2 participants rarely miss events, and the heavy Instagram users are satisfied. The pitch is for the underserved groups above, not everyone in El Paso, but eventually we hope that Instagram users would prefer the service too.

 That Juárez is in scope: We are not sure if Juárez would be included in the scope due to comments of people saying they don't care about events there; however, this could help us expand on the amount of users that would be interested.

 That the sample is representative of the city's needs. 

 3. What Didn't Work / What We Pivoted From

 App Candidate 1: Money already spoken for (dropped after Phase 1)

 Three of the five participants had abandoned manual expense logging, but nobody described the stated problem of not knowing how much income was already being spent.

 App Candidate 4: Market Master (dropped after Phase 1)

 Every answer was a hypothetical, so we didn't have any real data based on facts.

 App Candidate 5: Searching across streaming services (dropped after Phase 1)

 The strongest evidence of any candidate since most participants had paid twice for something they already had access to. We dropped it anyway because we couldn't get availability data across five services as a student team, and JustWatch/Reelgood already solve this for free.

 App Candidate 2: Eating toward a body goal (dropped after Phase 2)

 The team recorded one limitation at the time: every participant had been recruited because they already tracked macros, so the sample could confirm the problem but could not disconfirm it. Phase 2 fixed the sample, and the problem did not survive it. Of thirteen participants, three had never or barely tracked, three tracked loosely, two long-term app users find MyFitnessPal encouraging and sufficient, and four had tracked and quit for the logging-burden reasons in Finding 1. Not one described the specific problem we were looking to address.

 App Candidate 3: Event tracker (chosen project)

 Enough people, independently and without being prompted, described the same problem and asked for the same fix. That's a big enough gap in the market to justify choosing Candidate 3 over the other four candidates.

 Delivered by the team: Market Research, the owner's copy (https://gpi-portal.onrender.com/docs/sprint1-MARKET-RESEARCH.pdf) .

Gracias Por Invitar · Living Project Portal 
 G.P.I

 Team 9 Project Portal

 Gracias Por Invitar , Living Project Portal, Sprint 1
 Business Strategy
 The strategy-to-project chain: why this project earns the right to exist and what objective it serves.
 Version 1.1 , Final , revised Sep 21, 2026 Owner Oscar Vargas Team Samuel Alderete, Jazmin Huerta, Christian Lopez-Matulessy, Emmanuel Saenz, Oscar Vargas Course CS 4390/5388 Software Project Management , The University of Texas at El Paso , Fall 2026 Web https://gpi-portal.onrender.com/sprint-1/business-strategy/ The chain in one view

 Link Gracias Por Invitar 
 Market signal Local events are announced across dozens of social accounts; people hear about them from the people who happened to follow the right one, and often from the photos afterward. 
 Problem People find out about events after they have already happened. 
 Opportunity Nothing in the team's research serves the whole area in one place. A weekly listing page used to serve El Paso, and participants still miss it. 
 Business objective Become the place people in El Paso and Juárez check first for what is happening this week. 
 Project An events hub for El Paso and Juárez: one listing, by date, from arena concerts to farmers markets and car meets, with a feed personalized by interests and paid featured listings for organizers, within the charter's scope. 
 Success measures Below. The first targets are the Project Charter's; the Sprint 2 business case validates and extends them. 

 Why this project earns the right to exist

 The problem is real for a defined group. In Phase 2, six of twelve people described missing events they would have attended on a recurring basis, and seven of twelve, asked an open question about what they would change, asked for a single place to see what is coming. The people it fails hardest are the ones who rely on word of mouth and the ones with little or no social media. See the Market Research for the counts.

 The incumbents are not built for this job. Instagram shows people what they already follow. Google returns places, not events. Ticketmaster covers big shows. FitFam is one account's curation, known to the people who know it. Each is good at its own job and none of them is a listing of what is happening in El Paso this weekend.

 Demand for the specific shape has been demonstrated once already. One participant described a page that "would put all of the events that were going on every week," and that they used until it stopped. Another asked for "a weekly event round-up or calendar." The ask is not novel; it is unmet.

 It is buildable by this team in a semester. The core is still a listing with dates and categories. Personalization and paid listings are in the charter's scope, but they come after a reliable supply of events and a useful listing. The hard part is sourcing accurate event information across El Paso and Juárez, and that is a process and partnership problem the team can plan, not a technology the team cannot obtain (which is what stopped Candidate 5).

 Who it serves first

 People who rely on word of mouth , the largest group in the sample and the one with the strongest stories. Give them the thing they currently get from the friend who follows everything.

 People with little or no social media. For them there is currently nothing except a sign by the road.

 Event organizers and venues , who today advertise only to their existing followers. They are the supply side and the likeliest partners.

 The heavy Instagram user with a curated feed is not the first customer. They are served well enough by what they have and they will judge the product against it.

 The business objective

 Within the semester, launch a public event-discovery platform covering El Paso and Juárez that gives people advance notice of upcoming events and gives organizers a direct place to publish them. The Project Charter sets the first success criteria: organizer participation, advance notice, and interest in paid featured listings. The Sprint 2 business case tests those assumptions, refines the targets where needed, adds the business-case measures below (returning weekly visitors and events listed per week), and carries the go/no-go recommendation.

 Success measures

 Measure Why it matters Target 
 Organizer participation Sustainable supply, not team curation forever At least 20 El Paso and Juárez organizers post events by the end of the pilot run (Project Charter) 
 Advance notice The problem is information arriving too late to be useful; participants asked for about a week At least 80% of listed events are shown to users one week before the event (Project Charter) 
 Interest in paid featured listings Tests whether the charter's monetization idea has real organizer interest At least 2 event organizers express interest in paying for a featured listing during the pilot run (Project Charter) 
 Returning weekly visitors The habit the product is trying to create Set in the Sprint 2 business case 
 Events listed per week The product is only useful if it is more complete than a feed Set in the Sprint 2 business case 

 How it could sustain itself

 The Project Charter names paid featured or promoted listings as the monetization approach to test. That is a hypothesis, not a proven revenue stream: Sprint 2 evaluates whether organizers show enough interest to support it, and whether the other options the research points at, sponsorship by venues or the city's tourism office and promoted partnerships, should stay as alternatives. Every one of them depends on supply the team has not secured yet, which is why sourcing events is the first strategic risk below.

 What would make the team stop

 Kill criteria, so the go/no-go in Sprint 2 has something to test against:

 Events cannot be sourced reliably enough to be more complete than a good Instagram feed.

 Organizers will not submit, and manual curation by the team does not scale past the semester.

 Visitors do not come back the following week.

 Strategic risks

 Risk Effect First response 
 Sourcing: the listing is thinner than a curated feed The product loses to the incumbent it is trying to replace Start with a small number of categories and venues and be complete in those 
 Discovery: "how would people find out about the standardized way" Nobody visits the hub Distribution plan with organizers and the accounts people already follow 
 Scope breadth: two cities, personalization and paid listings Time goes to secondary features before the core listing is reliable The date-based listing first; personalization and paid listings in controlled increments, within the charter's scope 
 A free incumbent adds a city-wide listing The gap closes Speed, and organizer relationships that a platform does not have 

 Links

 Market Research : the evidence behind every claim above.

 Project Charter : scope boundary, constraints, assumptions, stakeholder register and success criteria.

 Project Charter
 Business objectives, scope boundary, constraints, assumptions, success criteria and stakeholders, as set and signed by the project manager.
 Version 1.2 , Final , revised Sep 21, 2026 Owner Emmanuel Saenz Team Samuel Alderete, Jazmin Huerta, Christian Lopez-Matulessy, Emmanuel Saenz, Oscar Vargas Course CS 4390/5388 Software Project Management , The University of Texas at El Paso , Fall 2026 Web https://gpi-portal.onrender.com/sprint-1/project-charter/ Project title GPI – Gracias Por Invitar 
 Project sponsor UTEP Computer Science Department 
 Project manager Emmanuel Saenz 
 Team members Jazmin Huerta, Samuel Alderete, Christian Lopez-Matulessy, Oscar Vargas 
 Date prepared 10 September 2026 
 Version 1.2 (the delivered file is numbered 1.0) 

 The charter was written by the project manager, who signed it on 21 September 2026. This page carries its full text and the PDF is printed from this page. The signed charter as delivered is kept alongside, as is the first delivery of 10 September , version 1.0.

 1. Business objectives

 Phase 2 showcased a repeatable problem: El Paso / Juarez residents missing out on events due to scattered listings across multiple platforms. GPI – Gracias Por Invitar will help solve this problem by providing centralized event discovery across both sides of the border, to give event-goers advance notice to plan and attend.

 Centralize events. Create a centralized platform for event promoters to publish events, removing the need for users to scatter across multiple platforms to stay informed.

 Monetize on event publications. Offer paid featured or promoted listings to venues and organizers, an extra channel to reach users and a source of recurring platform revenue.

 Promote marketing on events. Give organizers and small businesses a low-effort way to market their events.

 2. Scope boundary

 In scope

 A centralized event calendar

 An event feed listed by date (upcoming events)

 A feed personalized by interests and preferences

 Marketing of events on the platform

 Monetization of published events

 Out of scope

 Ticketing and payment processing

 3. Constraints

 Fixed semester timeline. The project is built through sprints, with no budget for sponsorship or paid licenses.

 Uneven data availability. Juarez and El Paso event information may be inconsistent or inaccurate, so analytics on the data may be limited.

 Event planners. The project depends on the availability and accuracy of local event information supplied by event planners, which may vary across Juarez and El Paso.

 4. Assumptions

 These assumptions are based on what the team heard in the Phase 2 interviews.

 Event organizers and venues will be willing to post on the platform instead of relying only on social media, and to update published events if any information changes.

 Users will be willing to make an account and set their interests so the event feed can be personalized.

 5. Success criteria

 Criterion Target or measure 
 Event listing for organizers At least 20 Juarez and El Paso organizers post events by the end of the pilot run 
 Advance notice for users At least 80% of events are shown to users one week before the event 
 Interest in paid featured listings At least 2 event organizers express interest in paying for a featured listing during the pilot run 

 6. Stakeholders

 Stakeholder Role and interest 
 Dr. Daniel Mejia Project sponsor. Provides course oversight and project coaching. 
 Emmanuel Saenz Project manager. Leads planning and team scheduling, and reports progress to the sponsor. 
 Jazmin Huerta, Samuel Alderete, Christian Lopez-Matulessy, Oscar Vargas Development team. Design, document and verify platform development. 
 El Paso and Juarez event-goers End users. Will use the final product for event listings. 
 Event organizers and venues End users. Will use the final product for event listings. 

 Approval

 Role Signature Date 
 Sponsor Pending 
 Project manager Emmanuel Saenz, signed in the delivered PDF Sep 21, 2026

Gracias Por Invitar · Living Project Portal 
 G.P.I

 Team 9 Project Portal

 Gracias Por Invitar , Living Project Portal, Sprint 2
 Estimation Appendix
 How the team is sizing Release 1: the methods, the ranges and the reasoning. Part 1 takes the outside view, from three similar products; Part 2 estimates the event-goer slice two ways and presents a provisional range of 394 to 852 hours.
 Version 1.0 , Final , revised Oct 5, 2026 Owner Christian Lopez-Matulessy Team Samuel Alderete, Jazmin Huerta, Christian Lopez-Matulessy, Emmanuel Saenz, Oscar Vargas Course CS 4390/5388 Software Project Management , The University of Texas at El Paso , Fall 2026 Web https://gpi-portal.onrender.com/sprint-2/estimation-appendix/ What this appendix is

 The course asks for the estimation methods used, the ranges produced and the reasoning behind them. This page records them in the order the team produced them. Part 1 is the team's completed worksheet, "A First Look at Your Project's Size", which takes the outside view: the team's own experience and three similar products, as comparators for analogous estimation. Part 2 is the team's completed activity "Estimate One Slice of Your Project": one slice of the product, estimated by function points and by analogy, with story points as a cross-check, and the range a sponsor reads.

 The entries are carried here as the team wrote them. In Part 1, two columns were tightened for the page: the evidence column cites the records in the interview evidence that each capability rests on, and each date in the comparators is matched to the listed source that states it, with the gaps marked. Part 2 is the team's submitted version of 30 September 2026, carried as submitted; the revision history below lists how it got there. The worksheet and the activity as delivered are the Team's PDFs above.

 Part 1: a first look at the project's size

 The outside view, before any counting: what Release 1 must do, the closest thing anyone on the team has built, and three real products that solve a problem close to GPI's.

 Step 1: what Release 1 must do

 Written as what the system must do, not how, from the charter's in-scope items and the strongest needs from the interviews. The hidden-work key: T, testing; S, security or privacy; I, integration with other systems; D, data (collection, cleaning, migration); H, hosting and deployment; U, usability and accessibility; O, documentation or training.

 # Capability (what, not how) Evidence (charter or interview) Hidden work 
 1 An event organizer can upload events on the online platform Project Charter , objective 1 (centralize events) and the in-scope calendar; P2-C3-10 U, O, D 
 2 An event organizer can pay for featured events on the online platform by day and time. Project Charter , objective 2 (monetize on event publications) and the in-scope monetization of published events U, O, D, H 
 3 Show a unified event calendar Interviews (Phase 2): P2-C3-01 , P2-C3-07 , P2-C3-10 , P2-C3-12 ; Project Charter , the in-scope centralized event calendar T, D, H, U 
 4 Events goers will be able to subscribe to events based on categories Interviews: P2-C3-11 , P2-C3-05 D, U, I 
 5 The system will show a personalized feed that shows events based on the user's interests Project Charter , the in-scope feed personalized by interests; interviews P2-C3-06 , P2-C3-11 , P2-C3-03 , P1-C3-02 T, D, S 
 6 The system will show an event feed listed by date Project Charter , the in-scope event feed listed by date; interview P2-C3-04 D, U, T 
 7 A user can save events they want to attend Interview P2-C3-02 S, D, U 
 8 An administrator can review and approve a submitted event before it appears publicly Project Charter , constraints: uneven data availability, and event planners S, D, T, O 

 Step 2: the outside view, the team's own experience

 The most similar thing anyone on the team has built before.

 Question Answer 
 What was it? KASAPro, the internal operations app Samuel built for KASA Contractors: job scheduling, route planning, and pricing. It is the closest match anyone on the team has built, a database-backed web app whose usefulness depends entirely on its records staying accurate and current, which is the same bet GPI is making on event data. 
 How long was it expected to take? One month 
 How long did it take? Three months 
 What took longer than expected? The pricing and routing comparison: the dual unload-site cost comparison with load-type filtering, which carries more rules than anything else in the app. Every new load type changed the comparison, so the logic kept being reworked after it was supposedly done. 

 Step 3: the outside view, similar products

 Three real products that solve a problem close to GPI's, at least one small and at least one big, measured from the start of development to the first public release. Under each entry, a source check notes which of the listed sources states each figure.

 Product A, small: Upcoming.org

 Field Entry 
 Product and company Upcoming.org, a community event calendar started by Andy Baio as a side project. Bought by Yahoo! in 2005. 
 Why it is similar to GPI A city-by-city listing of what is happening, so people hear about events before they happen. The same job as GPI, built by one person with no budget. 
 Development started January 2003 (notes from Baio's talk "A Tale of Three .Orgs," PDX Web Innovators, 4 June 2008; no Baio-written source for the start date, so treat it as secondhand) 
 First public release 19 September 2003 (Baio's own launch post on waxy.org) 
 Time to first release About 9 months, worked nights and mornings around a full-time job. Baio's own verdict: "Rough site launched. Barely functional." 
 What the first release included Anyone could add events they were going to, in fixed categories; see who else was going; browse by metro area; a friends list; RSS feeds. No API, tagging, email or SMS until March 2005. 
 Team size One at launch. Baio kept his day job until the acquisition; two partners joined later. 
 What worked Supply came from attendees posting what they were going to, not from promoters. Self-promotion was "banned entirely for its first two years." A city did not need broad coverage to be useful: "only 2 or 3 individuals" were enough to make a college town work. 
 What did not work After the founders left Yahoo! at the end of 2007, "the social features that made Upcoming unique were minimized, or removed entirely," and "spam, like creeping kudzu, was left unchecked." By 2009 "the only people using Upcoming were event promoters and spammers." A Kickstarter-funded rebuild funded 30 May 2014 did not relaunch until March 2017, about 34 months. 
 Sources waxy.org/2003/09/upcomingorg_lau/ ; waxy.org/2013/04/the_death_of_upcomingorg/ ; stubborndreams.me/2008/07/31/a-brief-history-of-upcoming-dot-org-by-andy-baio/ ; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upcoming 

 Source check. The January 2003 start, the nine months, the nights and mornings around a day job, "only 2 or 3 individuals" and the October 2005 acquisition are in the 2008 write-up of Baio's talk. The 19 September 2003 launch is Baio's own launch post, confirmed by Wikipedia. The end-of-2007 departure, the minimized social features, the spam and the 2009 line are in Baio's 2013 post. Wikipedia dates the Kickstarter campaign's launch to 7 May 2014. Not stated in any listed source: the "banned entirely for its first two years" quote, "Rough site launched. Barely functional.", the March 2005 feature dates, the 30 May 2014 funding date and the March 2017 relaunch.

 Product B, big: Do512

 Field Entry 
 Product and company Do512.com is the Austin event discovery platform created by the DoStuff media network, run by local teams in 20 cities. 
 Why it is similar to GPI It serves as a discovery platform that helps people stay up to date with local events and places, which is what GPI will try to achieve. 
 Development started It started in Austin, TX, in 2006. ("Meet Courtney Goforth of Do512", Voyage Houston) 
 First public release 2006 ("The Story", Do512.com). They founded DoStuff in 2010, which let them expand to more cities. ("Innovation Nation: DoStuff Media", Austin Monthly) 
 Time to first release Do512's first release took 1 month after they first came up with the idea. ("Innovation Nation: DoStuff Media", Austin Monthly) 
 What the first release included It started as a website that listed all happy hours around Austin, but it then expanded to include all sorts of events. ("The Story", Do512.com) 
 Team size Two people at first (Jimmy Stewart and Scott Owens). Soon after, they recruited their girlfriends, so it became a team of 4. 
 What worked Broadening the scope of the website (including all types of events, not just happy hours). Dynamic listings. Adding more people to the team. External users (venues, artists, event organizers) could upload and update their own events, that ensured the list was accurate and exhaustive. Partnered with local venues to offer free tickets to users who would rsvp to their events, creating a lot of engagement. Creating their media DoStuff label to be able to use the same technology in other cities. 
 What did not work Having a smaller team of people. Having the scope of the site be so narrow. Static website, because it led to inaccuracy and outdated data. The first few years the business was not making money, it took them a few years to gain revenue. 
 Sources crunchbase.com/organization/dostuff-media ; voyagehouston.com/interview/meet-courtney-goforth-do512-austin-texas/ ; austinmonthly.com/innovation-nation-dostuff-media/ ; do512.com/p/do512s-10-year-anniversary-the-story 

 Source check. The Voyage Houston interview states the 2006 start in Austin, the founders Jimmy Stewart and Scott Owens, and the happy-hours catalogue the site began as. The Austin Monthly article, Do512's own story page and Crunchbase refuse automated reading, so the one-month build, the team of four, the 2010 founding of DoStuff, the free-ticket partnerships and the revenue statement could not be checked from the portal; they stand on the worksheet's attribution to those pages.

 Product C, big: Fever

 Field Entry 
 Product and company Fever, founder by 4 individuals, is a personalized event discover web platform 
 Why it is similar to GPI Initially started as a event discovery for two cities, quickly grew into hundredths of cities/categories/events, matching out interest-based feed. 
 Development started 2012, New York, NY 
 First public release Released in 2014 simultaneously in New York and Madrid 
 Time to first release About 2 years. 
 What the first release included Personalized recommendations for entertainment, dining, and cultural events, live in two cities. 
 Team size 4 co-founders at launch 
 What worked Launching in two major cities (New York & Madrid) 
 What did not work Not documentation in the sources found. 
 Sources feverup.com/en/mexico-city ; newsroom.feverup.com/en-AU/about/ ; preqin.com/data/profile/asset/fever-labs--inc-/140163 

 Source check. The Preqin profile states that Fever Labs was founded in 2014, is headquartered in New York, and has four founders (Pep Gomez, Alexandre Perez Casares, Francisco Hein and Ignacio Bachiller Strohlein). The two Fever pages state no dates, founders, cities or team size. Not stated in any listed source: the 2012 start, the Madrid launch, the two years to first release, and what the first release included.

 Step 4: what the comparison says

 Which hidden-work letter appears most often, and did the similar products struggle with it? Data (D) appears the most often, which can be seen in all 8 capabilities. Do512 also struggled with static data which led to inaccurate and outdated listings. Upcoming.org also struggled with data quality and moderation, eventually dying out when unmoderated spam ruined the listings.

 How long did the similar products take, with how many people, and what does that suggest? Upcoming.org took roughly 9 months for a first release, with only one person. Do512.com took 1 month for the first release; initially it was two people, they then recruited two more people. Fever took about two years for the first release; there were four co-founders for the first release. Although we deployed a functional baseline website in one week after doing research, our comparables indicate that developing a production-ready first release would take about 6 to 12 months.

 One practice to copy and one mistake to avoid. Practice to copy: allow external users and organizers to directly submit and manage event content. Mistake to avoid: avoid static listings since it leads to inaccuracy and outdated data.

 Our comparables suggest a first release would take 6 to 12 months with a team of 5. 

 Part 2: one slice, estimated two ways

 The team's completed activity "Estimate One Slice of Your Project" (Lesson 9, Part 2), carried here as the team submitted it on 30 September 2026. One slice of the product is estimated twice, with two methods that start from different information; the two answers are compared, and a range is presented. The event supply follows the charter and the strategy: organizers post, the team curates at first, and no outside-source import is in the slice, so both methods estimate the same functions. The figures stay provisional on the rates: the function-point productivity rate and the analogous inputs are assumed, not measured. The team confirmed the seven story point values and verified the wage figure on 29 September 2026.

 Step 1: the slice

 Question Our slice 
 Slice name (one or two major parts) User and event-goer features 
 Why we chose it Event discovery is the central user experience. This coherent slice covers the calendar, date views, category preferences, saved events and search; organizer and admin flows are separate. 
 Screens or forms where users enter data Log in and user registration; the account settings page; the category ("interest") selection screen; the save event button 
 Reports, results or lookups users see Outputs: a feed ranked by the user's chosen categories. Personalization in this slice filters or orders events by user-selected categories; machine-learning and predictive recommendations are not included. Lookups: the calendar of El Paso and Juárez events, and the same events listed by date (one lookup, two presentations); the event details page (time, place, details); search results from the search bar; the saved events list; my account and chosen categories. 
 Data the slice stores Users; the user's preferences; events 
 Other systems it connects to None in this slice. Source of events: this slice reads a common GPI events catalogue. For Release 1, the Project Charter and the Business Strategy have organizers posting events, with the team curating at first, and this estimate takes that as the supply. 
 Out of the slice Organizers uploading or editing events; importing events from outside sources; paid featured listings for organizers; admin review and approval of submitted events; ticketing and payment processing (out of scope in the charter); email or push notifications about new events; social features, like a friends list or seeing who else is going 

 Stories in the slice. 

 User story MoSCoW Points 
 As an event goer, I can see a unified calendar of events across El Paso and Juárez. Must 8 
 As an event goer, I can browse upcoming events listed by date so I know what is on this weekend. Must 5 
 As an event goer, I can open an event and see its time, place and details. Must 3 
 As an event goer, I can create an account and subscribe to the event categories I care about. Must 8 
 As an event goer, I can see a feed ranked to the categories I chose. Should 5 
 As an event goer, I can save an event so I can come back to it later. Could 3 
 As an event goer, I can search for an event by name or keyword. Should 5 
 Total points 37 

 Points: on 29 September 2026 at 3:30 PM, the team reviewed and confirmed all seven user-story point values. The agreed values are 8, 5, 3, 8, 5, 3 and 5, totaling 37 story points. Search was added to the story table in an earlier revision after appearing among the slice lookups without a separate story. Capabilities 5 and 7 of the Part 1 list, the personalized feed and saved events, are Should and Could here: both are in scope for Release 1, and the Business Strategy sequences personalization after the core listing.

 Step 2: the two methods

 Analogous and function points. In the team's words: "Analogous method begins at the market research level where we identify facts such as failures and successes of a product. We can prove through research and facts about how an organization might have shipped a similar product and succeeded or failed. Function points, on the other hand, start from one's own design indicating count of inputs, results, lookups and data in our slices. Neither method uses the other's numbers, so if they agree, the agreement means something." Use-case points were not used. Story points (3C) were completed as a cross-check, not as a declared method.

 Step 3A: function points

 Category Count Weight Points 
 External inputs (EI) 4 4 16 
 External outputs (EO) 1 5 5 
 External inquiries (EQ) 5 4 20 
 Internal logical files (ILF) 3 10 30 
 External interface files (EIF) 0 7 0 
 Total function points 71 

 Rate: low 6 and high 12 hours per function point, the range from Part 2, Slide 15, since the team has no productivity history (assumption). Effort: 71 × 6 = 426 hours (low); 71 × 12 = 852 hours (high).

 The counts, itemized. External inputs (4): user registration, account settings update, category interest selection, and save event. Log in is listed as a screen in Step 1 but is not counted as an input, because it stores no business data of its own. External output (1): the category-ranked feed, which orders events against stored preferences and so derives data rather than returning it as stored, which is what separates an output from an inquiry on Slide 13. External inquiries (5): events listed by date, which the calendar presents in another form over the same data and processing and so is not counted again; the event detail page; search results; the saved events list; and the account and chosen categories view. Internal logical files (3): users, user preferences, and events. External interface files (0): the slice reads only the GPI catalogue; the outside source carried in the previous revision is out of the slice. Every item appears once and none is counted in two categories.

 Step 3C: story points, as a cross-check

 Input Value Note 
 Slice points 37 From the Step 1 story table 
 Team size 5 Five or six at most 
 Hours per person per sprint 20 Assumption 
 Velocity: low, middle, high 4, 6, 8 Assumptions until there is sprint data 
 Sprints needed (high to low velocity) 4.6, 6.2, 9.3 Slice points ÷ velocity 
 Effort in hours (low to high) 463 to 925 Sprints × team size × hours per person per sprint 

 Our assumptions: twenty hours per person per sprint is a two-week sprint at 10 productive hours a week each, alongside coursework. The velocities of 4, 6 and 8 points per sprint have nothing behind them: Slide 26 says real velocity needs at least three completed sprints by the same team, and we have run none. Effort is sprints × 5 people × 20 hours, so 100 team hours a sprint, giving 463 hours at the high velocity, 617 at the middle and 925 at the low. Low effort corresponds to the highest velocity.

 Step 3D: analogous

 Question Answer 
 Comparable product, team size, and time to first release Upcoming.org . One person (Andy Baio), about 9 months to first public release, 19 September 2003 (waxy.org launch post). 
 Person-months (team size × months) 1 × 9 = 9 person-months. Baio built it nights and mornings around a full-time job, so we assume 70 hours per person-month rather than 160 (assumption). That puts their first release at roughly 630 hours. 
 Fraction of their release our slice matches (low to high), and why 50 to 70 percent. Their first release was browse-by-metro listings in fixed categories, user-added events, attendee lists, a friends list and RSS. Our slice takes the browsing and listing side: their metro browse against our calendar and date list, their event page against ours, and their events-you-are-going-to list against our saved events. We add account preferences and a category-ranked feed, which their first release did not have. Later updates added an API, tagging, email and SMS (the sources we listed do not date them), and we found no source showing it ever carried a ranked feed, so we do not claim one. We leave out their event entry, attendee lists and friends list, which sit outside our boundary. Both methods now cover the same functions: our slice reads events from the GPI catalogue, as Upcoming's first release read the events its users had added, and the entry of events sits outside our boundary in both. 
 Team size adjustment and why Uplift of 25 to 35 percent. Upcoming was one person with no coordination cost at all. We are five, with 10 communication paths, so our effort per feature is higher than his. We did not scale from Fever's four founders, whose first release took about two years by our Part 1 worksheet (a figure the listed sources do not confirm), because that was a company rather than a side project and its effort already carries its own coordination. 
 Adjusted effort in hours (low to high) 630 × 0.50 to 0.70 = 315 to 441 hours. With the 1.25 to 1.35 uplift, 394 to 595 hours. Middle, at 60 percent and 1.30, is 491 hours. 
 Confidence, and why Medium. The comparable is the right shape, and the 19 September 2003 first release is grounded in Baio's own launch post on waxy.org. The January 2003 development start is secondhand, from one attendee's notes on a talk he gave in 2008, and we found nothing written by him giving that date. Beyond the dates, the 70 hours per person-month, the 50 to 70 percent fraction and the 25 to 35 percent uplift are all our modeling choices rather than recorded figures. The fraction moves the answer by about 40 percent across its range and the uplift by about 8 percent; the hours per person-month move it without limit: at 100 hours per person-month the range would be 563 to 851 hours, and at a full-time 160, 900 to 1,361. 

 Step 4: the team-size check

 Check Yes or no Why it matters 
 Our team is five or six people at most. Yes, a team of 5 Beyond six, split into two teams. 
 We counted our communication paths: n(n − 1) ÷ 2. Yes, 10 paths Five people share 10 paths; ten share 45. 
 We added explicit work for integrating the pieces of the slice. No; see the integration work below. Breaking work into pieces hides the cost of putting it back together. 
 We did not assume that more people means proportionally more output. Yes Coordination grows faster than headcount. 
 We estimated for the team we have. Yes Not for a larger team we wish we had. 
 We adjusted, not copied, timelines from much larger teams. Not applicable. Our comparable was one person, smaller than our team, so we scaled its effort up (3D) rather than copying a larger team's timeline down. Their effort includes their coordination costs. 

 Integration work (row 3). The answer is No because no separate hours were added for putting the pieces together. Coordination and technical integration are different things: the 25 to 35 percent uplift in the analogous estimate covers coordination among five people, and the 6 to 12 hour function point rate is an all-in rate from design through testing. The lines below are assumed inside that rate and inside the comparable's recorded effort, which included its own integration.

 Keeping organizer-entered dates, times, places and categories consistent across the two cities: assumed inside the function point rate.

 Wiring the calendar, detail page, ranked feed and saved events together: assumed inside the function point rate.

 End-to-end tests, data-failure handling and deployment: assumed inside the function point rate.

 Step 5: the comparison

 Function points Analogous 
 Estimate in hours (low to high) 426 to 852 394 to 595 
 Middle value in hours 639 (71 FP × 9 h) 491 
 Input that drives it most Productivity rate (hours per function point) Hours per person-month assumed for the comparable (70), then the fraction of the release matched 
 Measured or assumed? Assumed Assumed 

 Gap: larger middle value ÷ smaller middle value = 639 ÷ 491 = 1.30, an absolute difference of 148 hours.

 Do the two methods depend on the same assumption? No, the function points method starts from our internal design counts (inputs, reports, results, etc.) in Step 1, multiplied by productivity rates. The analogous method starts from external market historical data scaled to our scope and adjusted for 5-person team coordination costs.

 Which single input moves the answer most? The productivity rate in function points moves the estimate by 426 hours, from 426 at 6 h/FP to 852 at 12. In the analogous method, holding the coordination uplift fixed at 30 percent and moving the matched-release fraction from 50 to 70 percent takes the estimate from 409.5 to 573.3 hours, a difference of 163.8 hours. The full 394 to 595 range varies the uplift as well, between 1.25 and 1.35, so that wider 201.6 hour spread cannot be attributed to the fraction alone. The analogous method's lever is the 70 hours per person-month assumed for Baio's side project: at 100 hours per person-month the range would be 563 to 851 hours, and at a full-time 160, 900 to 1,361 hours, more than the fraction or the uplift can move it.

 What information would narrow the gap, and when could you get it? Our first one or two actual software-development sprints would give early effort observations, but they would not establish a reliable rate. We need hours recorded against completed stories, and Slide 26 sets at least three completed sprints by the same team before velocity means anything. Course-portal documentation sprints do not count as GPI development velocity. More data should narrow the 6 to 12 hour range; it will not eliminate the uncertainty.

 The team's explanation of the gap. Function point yielded a middle value of 639 hours, whereas the Analogous method yielded a middle value of 491 hours, creating a gap of 1.30x (under 2.0x). The primary driver of the gap is that our Function point estimate assumes a wide productivity rate of 6 to 12 hours per point due to lack of sprint data. Meanwhile, the Analogous method relies on our assumed Fraction of their release our slice matches and a 70-hour per person month. Both methods start from completely independent information, so the gap represents the distance between two assumptions we have never tested. The optional story-point cross-check gives 463 to 925 hours for the team's confirmed 37-point slice. Its result of 925 hours exceeds the two-method upper bound of 852 hours by 73 hours. Because the cross-check velocity is an untested assumption and story points are not a declared estimation method, this indicates upper-end uncertainty rather than automatically changing the formal range. What would narrow the gap is real hours logged against finished stories. Holding the coordination uplift at 30 percent and moving the feature match from 50 to 70 percent takes the analogous estimate from 409.5 to 573.3 hours, a swing of 163.8 hours. The wider 394 to 595 spread varies the uplift as well, so the fraction alone does not account for all of it.

 Step 6: the estimate

 Field Our estimate 
 Slice estimated User and event-goer features 
 Range in hours (low to high) 394 to 852 hours 
 Expected hours: (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6, and why we chose M (394 + 4 × 594 + 852) ÷ 6 = 603.67 expected hours. For M we took the midpoint of the lowest and highest ends of the range, which gave a first value M1 = 623, then the midpoint of the two methods' middle values, which gave M2 = 565. We settled on the midpoint of those two, M = 594. M = 594 is a planning judgment, not a measured value. We think an outcome near 594 hours is plausible because both methods rely on assumed data, and 594 sits in the middle, where neither method's weakness dominates. 
 Cost range and loaded rate used Base hourly wage: $51.36, for ZipRecruiter's "IT Software Engineer Salary in Texas" listing ( source ). The team verified the figure and job category on 29 September 2026 at 3:30 PM. Overhead: 20 percent, a team assumption, producing a loaded hourly rate of $61.63 (rounded). Low: 394 × 61.63 ≈ $24,282. Expected: 603.67 × 61.63 ≈ $37,204. High: 852 × 61.63 ≈ $52,509. 
 Calendar estimate in weeks, and hours per week assumed Expected: 12.07, about 12 weeks, at an assumed 10 productive hours per person per week. Low end: 394 ÷ 50 ≈ 7.9 weeks. High end: 852 ÷ 50 ≈ 17.0 weeks. This assumes all five people are available continuously at 10 productive hours a week. It is a production estimate for the slice. In Part 1, we estimated that it would take 6 to 12 months to produce a full first release; however, after Part 2 of the estimation analysis, 12.1 weeks corresponds to the time it would take to implement the event-goer slice alone, at the stated capacity. 
 Methods used Analogous and function points. Story points (3C) were completed as a cross-check, not as a declared method. 
 Key assumptions Productivity rate: 6 to 12 hours per function point, from Part 2, Slide 15; with no sprint history it is not measured. Scope: as listed in Step 1. 70 hours per person-month for Baio's side-project effort on Upcoming, rather than a full-time 160. Our slice is 50 to 70 percent of Upcoming's first release. A 25 to 35 percent coordination uplift for five people. 20 percent overhead on the ZipRecruiter hourly figure, a team assumption. 10 productive hours per person per week, which drives every week figure. Velocities of 4, 6 and 8 points per sprint in the story point cross-check. Event supply: organizer-posted events in a GPI-owned catalogue, with the team curating at first, as the Project Charter and the Business Strategy have it; no outside-source import is in this slice. The team reviewed and confirmed the seven story-point values (total 37) on 29 September 2026 at 3:30 PM. Story-point velocity (4, 6 and 8 points per sprint) remains an assumption because no completed software-development sprints have established historical velocity. 
 Team size assumed 5 team members 
 What would change this estimate Adding more productive hours per person. Adding an outside-source import to the slice. Further feeds of the same data add integration hours, not function points. Real productivity and velocity data after three completed sprints, which Slide 26 sets as the minimum. Scope changes. Team changes. 
 Date of this estimate 29 September 2026 

 What is still open

 Measured rates. The productivity rate and a real velocity come only from completed development sprints, at least three by the same team (Slide 26); until then every rate on this page is an assumption.

 What this range feeds next. The Project Budget prices it. The sponsor confirmed on 5 October 2026 that a Business Case and an ROI Analysis are not Sprint 2 deliverables, so the range's next use comes with a later sprint. The change log records how the range moved and what it affected.

 Project Budget
 The team's budget for the event-goer slice: the one-page summary a sponsor reads (603.67 hours, $58,868 requested, 12.1 weeks) and the ten steps behind it, from five cost-driving assumptions with owners through the staffing plan, labor at loaded cost and productive hours, a base build of $49,622 and two reserves to the time-phased request.

 The course's Session 11 activity, "Building the Budget", turns an estimate into money in ten steps: the assumptions the cost depends on, the work in packages, effort from more than one method, hours converted to FTE-months, a staffing plan by month, a loaded labor rate, the labor and everything else, the cost of ownership, the risks and the two reserves, and the budget time-phased into a request. The team's budget starts from the Estimation Appendix : the range of 394 to 852 hours for the event-goer slice, and the planning value of 603.67 hours.

 This page carries the two documents the team delivered, as the team wrote them. First the one-page budget summary of 6 October 2026, the version a sponsor reads. Then the ten-step budget of 4 October 2026 that supports it, step by step. The files are the Team's PDFs above. The charts are redrawn from the team's figures in the portal's palette, so they read in both themes and in print, and the revision history at the foot of the page records where the page and the delivered files differ.

 The budget on one page

 Cost-driving assumptions and owners

 Cost-driving assumption Owner 
 Slice boundary. Only the event-goer slice is priced: 7 stories, 37 points, 71 function points. Imports from outside sources are excluded; one import adds about 12 FP (108 h). Emmanuel Saenz, Project Manager

 Effort: two methods and the planning value

 Effort, two methods and the planning value: function points give 426 to 852 hours, the analogous method 394 to 595 hours, and the PERT planning value of 603.67 hours sits inside the first range, just above the second. 400 500 600 700 800 Function points 426 to 852 h Analogous 394 to 595 h Planning value 603.67 h team hours Effort, two methods and the planning value: function points give 426 to 852 hours, the analogous method 394 to 595 hours, and the PERT planning value of 603.67 hours sits inside the first range, just above the second. 
 Two independent methods. Function points start from our own design count; analogous starts from Upcoming.org scaled to the slice.  Top risks and the schedule gap

Closing the gap means a smaller slice or a longer timeline.

 Sources and sign-off

 Sources: GPI Session 11 Part 1 Budget, Steps 1 to 10 (the 11-page support document); budget figures are the final Step 10 values. Wage base: ZipRecruiter, IT software engineer salary in Texas . Analogous base: Upcoming.org history, sourced in the team's Session 9 estimation. Every other chosen number is a team assumption with the owner shown.

 Team sign-off: Team 9 approved all four items as written: the five assumptions and owners; the staffing split by month; the three risk chances and impacts; and the 5 percent management reserve.

 The ten steps behind it

 The support document: the team's completed "Building the Budget" activity of 4 October 2026, carried step by step as the team wrote it. The summary above takes its figures from the final Step 10 values.

 Estimate, budget, baseline

 Three different things. The Session 9 estimate becomes a budget only when someone with authority approves it, and the baseline is the version the team is held to.

 Estimate Budget Cost baseline 
 What it is A forecast of effort and cost, with a range The money leadership approves, including a cushion for surprises The approved month-by-month spending plan you measure against 
 Set by The project team The sponsor (the executive who pays) Built by the project manager, approved by the sponsor 
 GPI 394 to 852 hours = $32,377 to $70,014. Expected 603.67 hours = $49,607 (traced to Step 3 in this document) Requested: $58,868. Baseline: $56,065. Cushion: $2,803 (Step 10) $56,065: the $49,622 base build phased over 3 months (M1 $17,820, M2 $17,805, M3 $13,997), plus $6,443 contingency held back for named risks (Step 10) 

 Two ways to start a budget

 Top-down Bottom-up 
 How it starts From a number someone wants, such as a fixed date or a fixed dollar amount. From the list of work that has to be done, priced piece by piece. 
 GPI Project Charter : 8 weeks × 50 team-hours = 400 hours × $82.18 (per productive hour) ≈ $32,870 Seven work packages (37 points, 71 function points): 603.67 hours, $49,607 of labor plus $15 non-labor = $49,622 
 Use it for A quick reality check. It tells you what leadership hopes for. The budget you defend. It tells you what the work costs. 

 Build bottom-up, then set it beside the top-down number. The gap between the two is a finding, written up in Check 5 under Step 10.

 Step 1: what the cost depends on

 A cost-driving assumption is a statement that, if it turned out wrong, would change the cost. The team lists five, each with an owner.

 Assumption Why it drives cost Owner 
 In the event-goer slice, we include 7 stories, which are 37 points and 71 function points. Any outside-source imports are out. Everything outside the slice is unpriced. An import is 12 function points which equals about 108 hours. Emmanuel Saenz, Project Manager (charter scope) 
 Organizers post events into GPI-created catalogue, and the team curates it first, like how the charter and Business Strategy have it. Rules out imported work in the build and sets the curation hours in the operating cost. Oscar Vargas, Business Strategy Lead 
 Five people contributing 10 productive hours a week each, 50 team-hours a week, alongside coursework, for the whole build. Delivery work is split across developer, QA, UX and DevOps roles (65/17/10/8 percent, 545.17 delivery hours), and project management at 0.15 FTE is carved out of the 603.67 hours (58.5 hours). See the notes below. Sets the 12.1-week expectation and the monthly spend. Fewer hours contributed extends the calendar, but total hours remain the same. Pricing project management on top would add about 58.5 hours ($4,807). Jazmin Huerta, Market Research Lead 
 6 to 12 hours per function point, 70 hours per person-month for the comparable, with a 50 to 70 percent match and a 25 to 35 percent uplift. We have not measured any of these yet. Our whole range depends on these. After three sprints we'll replace them with our real numbers. Christian Lopez, Research Documentation Lead (Appendix owner) 
 Labor at $51.36 an hour (ZipRecruiter) = $106,829 a year. × 1.20 burden = $10,683 per FTE-month, or $82.18 per productive hour. Tools and hosting stay on free tiers, since the charter has no money for paid licenses. See the notes below. Every dollar amount is the number of hours times this rate. It means 15% of one full-time person each month, which is 0.15 × 130 = 19.5 hours a month, or 58.5 hours over 3 months. This is how the hours are carved out:

 Start with the total: 603.67 hours.

 Take the PM's share off first: 603.67 − 58.5 = 545.17 hours left for delivery.

 Split those 545.17 hours 65/17/10/8 among the delivery roles.

 The Session 9 estimate priced hours at $61.63, a loaded rate per paid hour; this budget prices them per productive hour, $82.18.

 Step 3: effort more than one way

 Three-point (PERT)

 E = (O + 4M + P) ÷ 6. O, the optimistic case, is 394 hours, if everything goes well. M, the most likely, is 594 hours. P, the pessimistic case, is 852 hours, if real problems hit. E = 3,622 ÷ 6 = 603.67 hours.

 Why E is above M: the bad case is farther from most likely than the good case is, so it pulls the answer up. Spread = (P − O) ÷ 6 = (852 − 394) ÷ 6 = 76.33 hours: a typical miss. Step 9 reuses it.

 The methods side by side

 Method Hours What it starts from 
 Bottom-up (the packages) 603.67 The seven work packages in Step 2 at 14.73 hours per story point across 37 points, plus 58.5 project management hours. The package hours were distributed from the PERT expected value, so this line is not an independent check on PERT. 
 Three-point (PERT) 603.67 O 394 from the analogous low. P 852 from 71 function points at 12 hours each. M 594 from the midpoint of the two method ranges (623) and the midpoint of their two middles (565). 
 Analogous 491 Upcoming.org: one person over about 9 months at an assumed 70 hours per person-month, so 630 hours, scaled by a 50 to 70 percent feature match and a 25 to 35 percent coordination uplift. Range 394 to 595.

Bottom-up and PERT are the same number by construction; the analogous estimate is the independent comparison. The planning value is 603.67 hours. 
 Do the methods land within 25 percent of each other? The rule of thumb: if they differ by more than 25 percent, find out why before pricing anything. The team's answer: not needed, the spread is 23 percent. The planning value of 603.67 hours sits 22.9 percent above the 491 hour analogous midpoint, inside the 25 percent rule.  Price the risks: the contingency reserve

 How to read it: expected monetary value (EMV) = chance × impact. It is an average, not a prediction: a risk either costs about its impact or nothing, and the reserve covers the expected total. The template asks for the top three risks at least.

 Cross-check: one PERT spread from Step 3 × the productive-hour rate = $6,273 (76.33 hrs × $82.18) of effort risk alone. Is the reserve at least that large? Yes, $6,443 is $170 more.

 Expected monetary value by risk, chance times impact: $3,061, $2,663 and $719, a contingency reserve of $6,443. $0 $1,000 $2,000 $3,000 Effort near pessimistic $3,061 Organizers don't post $2,663 Messy event data $719 EMV ($), total $6,443 Expected monetary value by risk, chance times impact: $3,061, $2,663 and $719, a contingency reserve of $6,443.

 Step 10: the budget, phased and requested

 Time-phasing places each cost in the month it is spent. Labor = FTE that month × $10,683 per FTE-month (Step 6), using Step 5's unrounded FTE of 1.667, 1.667 and 1.310. The $15 domain is bought in month 1. Contingency is held back until a named risk occurs, so this shows the base build only.

 Cumulative base spend by month: $17,820 after month 1, $35,625 after month 2, and the full $49,622 base build by the end of month 3. $0K $10K $20K $30K $40K $50K $60K M 0 M 1 M 2 M 3 M 4 M 5 M 6 $17,820 $35,625 $49,622 month Cumulative base spend by month: $17,820 after month 1, $35,625 after month 2, and the full $49,622 base build by the end of month 3. 
 The full budget request

 How to read it: each line stacks on the last. Base build is what you expect. Contingency covers named risks. Management reserve covers the unnamed.

 Building the request: the $49,622 base build, the $6,443 contingency that makes the $56,065 cost baseline, and the $2,803 management reserve that makes the $58,868 total request. $0K $10K $20K $30K $40K $50K $60K $70K Base build $49,622 Cost baseline $56,065 Total request $58,868 Base build Contingency Management reserve Building the request: the $49,622 base build, the $6,443 contingency that makes the $56,065 cost baseline, and the $2,803 management reserve that makes the $58,868 total request. 
 Five sanity checks

 Totals match. Add the staffing plan by month and compare it to Step 4. Ours: 4.64 FTE-months by month (1.667 + 1.667 + 1.310) = 4.64 FTE-months in Step 4.

 Labor share is plausible. Divide labor by the base build. Ours: $49,607 ÷ $49,622 = 99.97 percent. Nearly all cost is people because every tool and service stays on a free tier.

 Estimates agree. Compare the effort estimates. Ours: 491 to 603.67 hours, within 23 percent.

 Reserves trace to risks. Every contingency dollar links to a named risk in the Step 9 table. Ours: $3,061 + $2,663 + $719 = $6,443, all three named in the Step 9 table.

 Top-down comparison. Put the sponsor's number next to yours and explain the gap. Sponsor's number: 400 hours (8 weeks × 50 team-hours), about $32,870 of labor. Ours: 603.67 hours, $49,607 of labor. The gap is 203.67 hours, or $16,737, about 51 percent more. Eight weeks at our 50 team-hours a week only fits 400 hours, but the seven stories in the slice price at 603.67 hours, which takes about 12.1 weeks at that pace. To close the gap either the slice gets smaller or the timeline gets longer.

 Check 5 in action: the sponsor's number

 What did the sponsor ask for, in time or money? 8 weeks at 50 team-hours a week, so 400 hours (about $32,870). Our budget says the work is 4.64 FTE-months.

 People needed for 4.64 FTE-months: 1.66 full-time people over the plan's 2.8 months, or 2.51 over the sponsor's 8 weeks (1.85 months). 0.0 1.0 2.0 3.0 1.66 Our plan (2.8 months) 2.51 Sponsor's 8 weeks (1.85 months) Full-time people People needed for 4.64 FTE-months: 1.66 full-time people over the plan's 2.8 months, or 2.51 over the sponsor's 8 weeks (1.85 months). Communication paths, n(n − 1) ÷ 2: with five people there are ten pairs where a misunderstanding can happen. 0 10 20 30 1 2 3 3 6 4 10 5 15 6 21 7 28 8 Paths People on the team (the accent marks our 5) Communication paths, n(n − 1) ÷ 2: with five people there are ten pairs where a misunderstanding can happen. 

 4.64 FTE-months ÷ 2.8 months = 1.66 people. 4.64 FTE-months ÷ 1.85 months (the sponsor's time) = 2.51 people. Every pair of people is a path where a misunderstanding can happen. 5 people means 10 of them.

 What is still open

 The rates behind every figure are assumed, not measured: hours per function point, hours per person-month for the comparable, the match and the uplift, the burden factor, and 130 productive hours per FTE-month. The team replaces them with its own numbers after three sprints, and the budget moves with them.
